newsitem.title: UK: Czech crown Eurobond wagon reaches new frontier.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown Eurobond wagon reaches new frontier.

text.p: High-yielding Czech crown Eurobonds have welcomed in the new year with a stream of issues, and lead managers said demand for paper would remain strong.
The Czech crown's stability is boosting confidence and driving demand. "Investors are buying into a positive currency story," said Jan Pudil, a banker at WoodCommerz in Prague.
"For an interest rate of around 11 percent you are buying a currency that is 65 percent linked to the mark but yielding seven to eight percent above it," Pudil said.
With seven bonds totalling 9.0 billion Czech crowns ($330 million) launched already this year, the sector has eclipsed other emerging currencies.
A syndicate official at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said it was unlikely the crown's bubble would burst.
"Political risk in the Czech Republic is quite low and although there might be some (currency) depreciation, it is totally different to South Africa, for example," he said.
Buyers of rand Eurobonds issued in 1995 lost around 30 percent in dollar terms following a slide in the currency.
Among the recent crown bonds was a 2.0 billion crown one-year deal for the Inter-American Development Bank lead managed by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Around 90 percent of Czech crown bonds were bought by retail investors from Germany, Benelux and Swiss buyers, DMG said.
The crown came under pressure last week on fears about the growing Czech current account.
"This worry was dismissed when the governor of the Czech National Bank said (last week) that curing the deficit by devaluation would be a stupid idea," said Pudil at Woodcommerz.
Since then the Czech crown has strenghened by one percent.
The CNB fixed the mark/dollar basket yesterday at rates that implied a 3.72 percent deviation from the midpoint, up from 2.78 percent on December 31.
But with an eight percent difference between mark and crown Eurobond yields, Pudil said even if there was depreciation, "there was still significant room for profit taking".
"There are more deals in the pipeline" he added. An inverted Czech crown yield curve means higher coupons are available at shorter maturities.

"There is most demand for one-year paper, where there is also very good arbitrage. There is also demand for two- or three-year paper but it is slower there," the Deutsche syndicate manager said. ($1 = CZK 27.3)
